content: The use of intranasal metoclopramide or interacting drugs should be carefully evaluated based on the importance of the drug to the patient. Below are specific interactions and recommendations for various drugs when used with intranasal metoclopramide: 1. Duloxetine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. It is recommended to avoid this combination or use an alternative drug. 2. Efavirenz and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): These drugs may increase each other's effects. Avoid concurrent use or consider an alternative therapy. 3. Entacapone and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): The combination may lead to increased effects of both drugs. Avoid or substitute with an alternative medication. 4. Epinephrine (Intranasal) and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Epinephrine may alter nasal mucosa for up to two weeks, increasing systemic absorption of nasal products. Use caution and monitor closely. 5. Escitalopram and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may potentiate each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 6. Esketamine (Intranasal) and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): The combination may increase the effects of both drugs. Avoid or substitute with an alternative. 7. Ethanol and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Alcohol may enhance the effects of metoclopramide. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 8. Fluoxetine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Fluoxetine can increase metoclopramide levels by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism. Avoid concurrent use or consider an alternative. 9. Fluphenazine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): This combination increases the risk of toxicity, including tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid or use an alternative. 10. Gabapentin and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 11. Insulin (Various Types) and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Increased gastrointestinal motility caused by metoclopramide may enhance food delivery to the intestines, potentially raising blood glucose levels. Monitor blood glucose closely and adjust insulin dosage as needed. 12. Isocarboxazid and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Metoclopramide may enhance the hypertensive effects of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 13. Haloperidol and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): This combination increases the risk of additive effects, including tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid or substitute with an alternative. 14. Levodopa and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): These drugs have opposing effects on dopamine, potentially exacerbating symptoms such as parkinsonism or reducing therapeutic efficacy. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 15. Linezolid and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Metoclopramide may enhance the hypertensive effects of monoamine oxidase inhibitors. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 16. Loperamide and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Loperamide may reduce the systemic absorption of metoclopramide by impairing gastrointestinal motility. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects. 17. Lorcaserin and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Lorcaserin may increase metoclopramide levels by inhibiting CYP2D6 metabolism. Avoid concurrent use or consider an alternative. 18. Loxapine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): This combination increases the risk of toxicity, including tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid or use an alternative. 19. Lurasidone and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): The combination may lead to additive toxic effects, including tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid or substitute with an alternative. 20. Methadone and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 21. Monoamine Oxidase Inhibitors (e.g., Isocarboxazid, Linezolid) and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Metoclopramide may enhance hypertensive effects. Avoid concurrent use or consider an alternative. 22. Levetiracetam and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may increase each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 23. Lithium and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 24. Methscopolamine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Methscopolamine may reduce the systemic absorption of metoclopramide by impairing gastrointestinal motility. Monitor for reduced therapeutic effects. 25. Loratadine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 26. Lorazepam and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 27. Loxapine (Inhaled) and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): This combination increases the risk of additive toxic effects, including tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid or substitute with an alternative. 28. Lurasidone and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): The combination may lead to additive toxic effects, including tardive dyskinesia and neuroleptic malignant syndrome. Avoid or substitute with an alternative. 29. Levodopa (Inhaled) and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): These drugs have opposing effects on dopamine, potentially exacerbating symptoms such as parkinsonism or reducing therapeutic efficacy. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 30. Methyldopa and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. 31. Metyrosine and Metoclopramide (Intranasal): Both drugs may enhance each other's effects. Avoid this combination or use an alternative. In summary, the concurrent use of intranasal metoclopramide with many drugs requires careful consideration due to potential interactions that may increase toxicity, reduce therapeutic efficacy, or exacerbate adverse effects. In most cases, alternative therapies should be considered, and close monitoring is recommended when co-administration is unavoidable.
